record.program_name: Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA), Madera County formula allocation
record.administering_agency: Madera County Community and Economic Development Department
record.typical_award_size: HCD formula allocations to the County: $226,380 (CY 2024) and $238,273 (CY 2025), with an estimated $1,414,875 for the 2024-2028 cycle; the City of Madera receives its own allocation ($296,439 in 2024, $317,530 in 2025; estimated $1,852,744 for 2024-2028). The County's PLHA five-year plan and activity choices were not located (County website blocked).
record.affordability_requirement: PLHA Guidelines Section 301: rental activities must be affordable to extremely low, very low, low or moderate income households (up to 120% AMI), and workforce rental and ownership activities may serve households up to 120% AMI; plans must prioritize households at or below 60% AMI. Rental projects need a 55-year regulatory agreement and PLHA must be a low-interest deferred loan to the sponsor.
record.next_deadline: No County NOFA. Confirm plan activities with Community and Economic Development ((559) 675-7821).
record.layering_notes: Madera County is a small non-entitlement county: the Community and Economic Development Department (planning, state CDBG and HOME applications) and Behavioral Health Services (BHSA, bridge housing) are the only County housing actors, the Housing Authority of the City of Madera (HACM) is the PHA for the county, and the Fresno Madera Continuum of Care (CA-514, led by Fresno County) handles HHAP and CoC funds. There is no County housing trust fund, NOFA, inclusionary ordinance or impact fee waiver program. The City of Madera is a separate CDBG and HOME entitlement with its own PLHA plan (Pass 3). maderacounty.com blocks automated access (403 on pages and documents), the PrimeGov and IQM2 portals returned no 2026 meetings, and Board agendas were read from PDFs mirrored on maderacountywater.com; other sources were HCD allocation tables, maderaha.org, zoneomics (County Code Title 18), CEQAnet and press coverage. Confirmation needed: at roughly $230,000 a year the County PLHA cannot anchor a development loan and is probably directed to homeless services; the plan document should be requested from the County. Source is HCD's 2024-2028 PLHA formula allocation NOFA tables.
record.cycle_notes: HCD releases each calendar-year allocation to the County, which applies on a rolling basis under its five-year plan; CY 2024 funds must be requested by February 2028 and CY 2025 by February 2029. No County NOFA to developers was found.
record.prevailing_wage_basis: Neither the 2019 PLHA Final Guidelines nor the 2024-2028 PLHA Formula Allocation NOFA states a prevailing wage requirement; coverage would depend on Labor Code 1720 for the specific project.
record.audit_note: Award figures confirmed in the HCD NOFA tables; AMI corrected from 80% to the Section 301 limits (moderate income up to 120% AMI, 60% AMI priority); prevailing wage reset to unclear because no rule was cited. County plan activities still unconfirmed, so eligible_project_types remain unverified.

record.prevailing_wage_basis: Only the general Labor Code 1720(b) definition applies; outcome depends on 1720(c) exemptions and project facts. HCD 2024-2028 PLHA Formula Guidelines (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/grants-and-funding/plha/2024-2028-plha-formula-guidelines.pdf) contain no prevailing wage, Davis-Bacon or Labor Code 1720 provision; the HCD PLHA FAQ (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/grants-and-funding/plha/cycle-2-nofa-faq.pdf) says only that HCD programs require compliance with applicable law including prevailing wages unless the project meets a Labor Code 1720(c) exception as determined by DIR. PLHA loans and grants are public funds under 1720(b)(1) and (b)(4) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720), but 1720(c)(5)(E) (below-market loans with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI), 1720(c)(5)(C) (mortgage, down payment or single-family rehab aid to a household) and 1720(c)(3) de minimis can apply. Davis-Bacon applies only if HOME (12+ HOME units, 24 CFR 92.354) or CDBG (8+ units, 24 CFR 570.603) is layered. The County PLHA plan and uses were not found, so whether any PLHA dollars fund construction is unknown.

record.program_name: Affordable Housing Density Bonus (FMC Chapter 15, Article 22) with TOD Height and Density Bonus (Article 21) and Housing Element Program 9 by-right approval
record.administering_agency: City of Fresno Planning and Development Department
record.typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. Article 22 implements Gov. Code 65915 for projects of 5 or more units (State law governs on conflict). Article 21 adds a discretionary TOD bonus of up to 100% more density and 25% more height in MX or CMS districts within 500 feet of a BRT station or half mile of Manchester Transit Center, combinable with the affordable bonus. Program 9 text amendment (P26-01326, 2026) makes projects with at least 20% lower-income units by-right on reused housing element sites.
record.affordability_requirement: State density bonus thresholds (e.g., 5% very low or 10% low income for a 20% bonus); covenants per Article 22 (at least 30 years in local text, 55 years under current State law for rentals). Fresno has no inclusionary requirement; FMC 15-2201(E) bars adopting one until the 2014 General Plan is superseded.
record.layering_notes: Local text predates recent State amendments, so the State statute controls bonus percentages and concessions. TOD stacking is a Fresno-specific advantage on Blackstone and Ventura/Kings Canyon BRT corridors. No density cap on mixed-use zones since 2022. No inclusionary fund exists to tap. Code read on the zoneomics mirror (City code host not used).
record.audit_note: Nov 9, 2026 spot check: Article 22 (5+ units, 30-year local covenant, 15-2201(E) bar on inclusionary) and Article 21 TOD bonus (MX or CMS, 500 feet of BRT or half mile of Manchester Transit Center, up to 100% density and 25% height) match the zoneomics mirror only; municode returns 403. Program 9 text amendment P26-01326 confirmed on City Legistar (file ID 26-560, Planning Commission June 3, 2026). Mirror-only source for the code text does not support verified.
record.prevailing_wage_basis: Labor Code 1720(a)(1) (california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720): public works means construction paid for in whole or in part out of public funds. A density bonus under Gov. Code 65915 grants units, concessions and waivers of standards, not public funds, so the bonus itself does not trigger prevailing wage. Wages may still apply through other public financing or through streamlining laws that require them (for example SB 423 or AB 2011).

record.program_name: Reedley Impact Fee Reduction Incentive Program (Resolutions 2019-009 and 2022-060) and affordable housing fee deferrals (Housing Element Programs 7 and 17)
record.administering_agency: City of Reedley Community Development Department and City Council
record.typical_award_size: Location-based reduction of development impact fees under the Impact Fee Reduction Incentive Program (Resolution 2022-060): Infill Area fees 25% below Expansion Area and City Center fees 50% below. 2022 multifamily impact fees per unit: $17,569 Expansion Area, $13,177 Infill Area, $8,785 City Center. Regional Transportation Mitigation fee is reduced for affordable units ($821 per affordable multifamily unit). Development impact fee deferral program (approved May 26, 2015): applicant pays a nonrefundable 20% of impact fees at building permit application and the remaining 80% before final inspection. Housing Element Program 7 also commits to continued fee reductions and deferrals for affordable and special-needs projects and lists reduced water and wastewater connection fees as a flexible standard.
record.per_unit_cap: Equal to the reduction; City Center saves about $8,785 per multifamily unit versus Expansion Area.
record.affordability_requirement: Area-based reduction has no affordability requirement; deferrals and further reductions are for lower-income and special-needs projects (details not codified).
record.next_deadline: Housing Element Program 17 called for a fee review with multifamily developers by December 2024 and a revised fee schedule by December 2025; outcome not confirmed.
record.layering_notes: Source is the City's adopted 2023-2031 Housing Element (Appendix 1L, adopted April 9, 2024, found in substantial compliance by HCD April 24, 2024), not the resolutions themselves. reedley.ca.gov could not be opened (TLS handshake failure), so the current fee schedule and any 2025 fee update were not verified. City Center sites stack the 50% fee reduction with State density bonus and County HOME/PLHA (Urban County) and Fresno Housing PBVs.
record.audit_note: Housing Element Appendix 1L supports the area reductions, 2022 fee amounts, the 2015 deferral terms and Resolution 2022-060; it does not mention Resolution 2019-009. reedley.ca.gov failed TLS handshake on 2026-11-08 so the current fee schedule and any December 2025 fee revision under Program 17 could not be checked. Prevailing wage: Labor Code 1720(b)(4) treats reduced or waived fees as public funds, but leginfo returned 403 and no City or DIR rule on these fee programs was read, so the trigger stays unclear.
record.prevailing_wage_basis: No program-specific prevailing wage rule is recorded for this program. Resolution 2022-060 sets lower impact fees by location (Infill 25 percent and City Center 50 percent below Expansion Area), and the Housing Element offers affordable housing fee deferrals; whether a location-based schedule is a reduction below fair market value is unsettled. Labor Code 1720(b)(4) (https://california.public.law/codes/labor_code_section_1720) counts fees paid, reduced, charged at less than fair market value, waived or forgiven by a political subdivision as public funds, so this relief can make a project paid for in part with public funds. Coverage then turns on project facts and 1720(c): (c)(1) private residential projects on private property not built under an agreement with a state agency, successor agency or housing authority, (c)(3) de minimis (subsidy under $600,000 and under 2 percent of total project cost), and (c)(5)(E) where the public participation is below-market loans on a project with at least 40 percent of units restricted 20 years at or below 80 percent AMI. Other public funds in the deal often decide the question.

record.program_name: Sanger affordable housing impact fee deferrals and reductions (Housing Element Programs 7, 15 and 19)
record.administering_agency: City of Sanger Community Development Department
record.typical_award_size: Case-by-case deferral or reduction of City development impact and permit fees for affordable, special-needs and farmworker projects, with priority processing on large sites. Baseline City impact fees (2021): about $18,600 per 1,000 sq ft multifamily unit (sewer $2,724, treatment $5,780, collection $1,356, water $1,397, storm drain $2,290, traffic $1,592, recreation $631, police $1,230, fire $1,270, solid waste $330), plus Sanger Unified school fee $4.79 per sq ft.
record.affordability_requirement: Lower-income, special-needs or farmworker housing; terms negotiated per project (not codified).
record.next_deadline: Program 19 called for meeting multifamily developers by December 2024 and revising fees by December 2025; Program 15 incentives for large sites by mid-2025. Outcomes not confirmed.
record.layering_notes: Source is the City's 2023-2031 Housing Element (Appendix 1N, adopted September 5, 2024, found in substantial compliance by HCD October 4, 2024), not a fee resolution. ci.sanger.ca.us opened but no fee deferral policy page or council resolution was found; confirm terms with the Community Development Department.
